title: Extension Cord Safety on the Jobsite
summary: Loose, damaged extension cords cause trips, shocks, burns, and even heart failure. This talk covers inspecting cords, using GFCIs, and what not to do with cords.
talking_points: Inspect every extension cord before use for damage and missing grounding prongs.
Use a Ground Fault Circuit Interrupter (GFCI) to protect against electrical faults.
Keep cords out of foot traffic to prevent trips and cord damage.
Do not use an extension cord where it is hard to inspect, where damage is likely, or as a substitute for permanent wiring.
Do not use a metal outlet box, Romex, or nonmetallic cable as an extension cord.
Do not staple or nail cords in place, and do not join several cords together - use one cord long enough for the job.
site_hazards_to_check: Cords with cuts, cracked insulation, or missing ground prongs
Cords run through walkways, doorways, or standing water
No GFCI protection on the circuit or cord
Multiple cords chained together, or cords stapled or nailed down
Extension cords used in place of permanent wiring
discussion_questions: How do you check a cord before you plug it in?
Where is the GFCI on this circuit, and how do you test it?
What is wrong with linking two shorter cords together?

flags: OSHA mapping verified accurate: 1926.404 (wiring design and protection, incl. GFCI at 404(b)(1)) and 1926.405 (flexible cords/extension cords at 405(a)(2) and (g)). Inspect before use, GFCI protection, no chaining cords, no substitute for permanent wiring, no stapling/nailing - all consistent with the standard. No tolerance issues.
